reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Presents with a red, painful, watery eye, photophobia, and blurred vision, often preceded by mild irritation
The classic sign is a branching dendritic epithelial ulcer with terminal end-bulbs that stains with fluorescein, with the ulcer bed highlighted by rose bengal or lissamine green
Reduced corneal sensation is a valuable clue to a herpetic cause
Disease may be epithelial (active viral replication), stromal (immune-mediated, with the risk of scarring and neovascularisation), or endothelial (disciform keratitis)
Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated in active epithelial (dendritic) disease as they promote unchecked viral replication and can enlarge the ulcer into a geographic form
Epithelial disease is treated with topical or oral antiviral therapy; stromal and endothelial immune disease requires cautious steroids under antiviral cover and specialist supervision
Recurrences are common because the virus remains latent in the trigeminal ganglion; repeated episodes cause cumulative scarring and neurotrophic changes
Long-term oral antiviral prophylaxis reduces recurrence in patients with frequent episodes
reference.pathophysiology: Herpes simplex keratitis is caused by herpes simplex virus, usually type 1, which after primary infection establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion. Reactivation, precipitated by stress, illness, ultraviolet light, or immunosuppression, sends the virus along sensory nerves to the cornea. Active viral replication in the epithelium produces the dendritic ulcer. Persisting viral antigen and the host immune response drive stromal inflammation (immune stromal keratitis) and endothelial disease (disciform keratitis), which can cause oedema, scarring, neovascularisation, and thinning. Repeated episodes and antiviral toxicity contribute to reduced corneal sensation and a neurotrophic cornea.
additionalDifferentials: Acanthamoeba keratitis (especially in contact lens wearers)
Healing epithelial defect with a pseudodendrite
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein and rose bengal or lissamine green staining
Testing of corneal sensation before instilling anaesthetic
Corneal scrape for viral PCR or culture in atypical or unclear cases
Assessment of stromal involvement, endothelial oedema, and intraocular pressure
Consideration of immune status in severe or bilateral disease
redFlags: A dendritic (or geographic) ulcer, which mandates avoidance of topical steroids in active epithelial disease
Worsening or enlarging ulcer after steroid exposure suggesting steroid-driven progression
Stromal necrosis, thinning, or a neurotrophic non-healing defect threatening perforation
Deep central scarring or dense keratitis causing significant visual loss
reference.prognosis: Isolated epithelial disease usually heals with antiviral treatment, but recurrent stromal disease can cause progressive scarring, neovascularisation, and neurotrophic complications with permanent visual loss; prophylaxis improves long-term outcomes.
pitfalls: Prescribing topical steroids for an undiagnosed red eye and worsening a dendritic ulcer
Mistaking a herpetic dendrite for a healing abrasion or zoster pseudodendrite
Overlooking reduced corneal sensation as a diagnostic clue
Failing to consider prophylaxis in patients with frequent recurrences
